title: Simple Verses XVI
text:
At the fretted window ledge

of the Moorish casement, pale

as the moon, a lover lingers,

lost in thought.


Pale upon her turtledove-

gray and crimson silken couch,

Eva, silent, plucks a violet

petal by petal into her tea.
editorial_note: The compact scene and its color contrasts take precedence over forcing the original enclosed rhyme.

title: Homeland in the Flowers
text:
Why do you wither, generous violets,

given me in bitterness by a merciful hand?

Timorous flowers, you give my soul a homeland—

you shall not wither in my memory!
editorial_note: Patria retains its political and intimate force as homeland; pía is rendered through mercy rather than piety alone.

title: Simple Verses XL
text:
My friend the painter paints

his great golden angels,

kneeling upon clouds,

with suns all around them.


Let his brushes paint for me

the timid little angels

who, in their mercy, brought me

their two bouquets of carnations.
editorial_note: The contrast between monumental angelones and tender angelitos is preserved through great and little.

title: Simple Verses XXXVI
text:
Now I know: out of flesh

a flower can be made; with love's

power, a heaven can be made—

and a child!


Out of flesh are also made

the scorpion, and likewise

the worm inside the rose,

and the terrifying owl.
editorial_note: The repeated made out of flesh holds together creation's tenderness and menace.

title: I Grow a White Rose…
text:
I grow a white rose

in July as in January,

for the faithful friend

who offers me an open hand.


And for the cruel one who tears out

the heart by which I live,

I grow neither thistle nor nettle;

I grow the white rose.
editorial_note: The plain diction and repeated final gift are preserved; franca becomes open, carrying candor and generosity.

title: Simple Verses XII
text:
I was rowing in the boat

across the beguiling lake,

with the sun all pure gold

and more than one sun in my soul.


Then suddenly, there at my feet,

insulted by the stench, I saw

a dead fish, a reeking fish,

in the rowing boat.
editorial_note: The abrupt fall from golden transcendence to bodily disgust remains deliberately comic and harsh.

title: Simple Verses XIV
text:
I can never forget

that little autumn morning

when a new shoot sprang

from the poor severed branch.


That little morning when, in vain,

beside the cold stove,

a girl in love

held out her hand to the old man.
editorial_note: The repeated diminutive morning carries tenderness into the stark human tableau.

title: Simple Verses XX
editorial_note: The deliberately circular betrayal and consolation are kept, along with the airy instability of the opening.

title: Simple Verses XXIII
text:
I want to leave this world

through its natural door:

in a cart of green leaves

they must carry me to die.


Do not set me in the darkness

to die as a traitor dies;

I am good, and as a good man

I shall die facing the Sun!
editorial_note: The civic declaration remains direct, with Sun capitalized to retain its emblematic radiance.

title: Simple Verses XXIX
text:
By law, the king's portrait

is borne on the paper of state;

the child was shot

by the rifles of the king.


By law, the king's saint's day

must be celebrated; at the holy feast,

the child's sister sings

before the portrait of the king!
editorial_note: The repeated law and king preserve the poem's bitter machinery of state violence and ritual.
